strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/r-3b30f255031c4d37/reviews/review-experiment-jvmxpr2x/call-81a87e82e0864b40a0f902cb7ee65336/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} addresses an important problem: grounding medical-AI decisions in clinical knowledge and explicit quantitative evidence rather than relying solely on end-to-end MLLM predictions.

The task-level retrieval/planning and case-level tool-execution structure is intuitive and modular. Intermediate outputs such as segmentation masks, vCDR, ejection fraction, ventricular dimensions, and indicator-level decisions could improve auditability.

Experiments cover both 2D fundus imaging and 3D echocardiography, compare two decision mechanisms, and include indicator-combination ablations. The results provide a preliminary signal that specialized tools can improve over direct zero-shot MLLM inference.
The architecture and example workflow are communicated clearly through readable figures and tables.
weaknesses: The experimental protocol is critically underspecified. There are no train/validation/test splits, sample counts per split, patient-level separation for MITEA's 536 scans from only 143 subjects, training data for the task-specific adapters, or explanation of whether dataset masks were used during development or inference. Leakage and test-set tuning therefore cannot be ruled out.

Reproducibility is inadequate: the promised code URL is blank, and the paper omits prompts, model/API versions, decoding settings, preprocessing, checkpoint details, random seeds, retrieval configuration, and the generated diagnostic plans.

Comparisons are not controlled. MedAgent-Pro receives specialized or fine-tuned tools and, for echocardiography, structured 3D processing, whereas MLLMs receive raw images or three randomly selected slices. There is no strong supervised classifier, segmentation-plus-fixed-rule pipeline, or other tool-augmented agent evaluated under the same inputs and split. The REFUGE2 leaderboard AUC comparison is not shown to use the same evaluation protocol, and the heart experiment lacks relevant task-specific baselines.

The so-called MOE decider is a weighted sum of discretized indicators rather than a conventional mixture-of-experts model. How the LLM chooses weights and how the threshold is selected are unspecified; without held-out selection and calibration, the reported accuracy and AUC are not trustworthy.

The claimed benefit of the agentic design is not isolated. There are no RAG-versus-no-RAG, generated-plan-versus-fixed-plan, orchestrator, coding-agent, or tool-quality ablations. Retrieval accuracy, citation faithfulness, plan consistency, and robustness to tool failures are never measured.

Several clinical details undermine the evidence-based claim. Figure 3 proposes confirming visual-field defects from eye photographs, which requires an appropriate functional test, while the heart example concludes hypertrophic cardiomyopathy from low LVEF and ventricular dilation without presenting the necessary wall-thickness evidence. A universal vCDR threshold is also an oversimplification.

The component outputs driving the diagnosis are not clinically validated. Segmentation performance and derived-measurement error are unreported, and REFUGE2 does not provide ground truth for all claimed indicators such as hemorrhage and peripapillary atrophy. Table 3 consequently measures how indicator heuristics predict the disease label, not whether those indicators were detected correctly.

The central reliability and interpretability claims receive no rigorous evaluation: there is only an illustrative case, with no clinician study, expert audit, explanation-faithfulness test, calibration analysis, abstention analysis, or systematic error analysis. Human validation is deferred to future work.

The empirical scope is narrow—two diseases and one dataset per disease, with no external-site or distribution-shift evaluation. The glaucoma experiment principally uses one fundus modality, so the broad claims about multi-modal diagnosis and generalizable task-level planning are not established.

Metrics are insufficiently specified, GPT-4o refusals are replaced by missing scores rather than evaluated through accuracy-coverage measures, and no confidence intervals or statistical tests support claims of significant improvement.

The architecture mainly combines established RAG, tool orchestration, and thresholded indicator aggregation; methodological novelty is limited. More importantly, the paper contains no substantive discussion of clinical safety, subgroup bias, privacy, accountability, human oversight, or harms from false diagnoses despite suggesting autonomous diagnosis. These evaluation, reproducibility, and safety deficiencies make the submission noncompetitive for a top-tier venue.

Given the medical setting, the ethics and safety discussion is inadequate: there is no meaningful analysis of patient-data governance, demographic bias, automation risk, unsafe false negatives, or appropriate human oversight. Overall, the promising results are too confounded and underdocumented to support acceptance at a top-tier venue.
